# Proof

We show that $A$ has full Lebesgue measure in $[0,1]$, i.e., $\lambda(A)=1$.

## Setup

Every irrational $x\in[0,1]$ has a unique infinite continued fraction expansion $x=[0;\,a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots]$ with $a_i\in\mathbb{N}^+$. Since the rationals have Lebesgue measure $0$, it suffices to work with irrationals.

The **Gauss map** $T(x)=\{1/x\}$ on $(0,1]$ preserves the Gauss measure $\mu$ with density $\frac{1}{\ln 2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+x}$, which is mutually absolutely continuous with Lebesgue measure (with bounded Radon–Nikodym derivative). The continued fraction digits are $a_n = a_1\circ T^{n-1}$, and the sequence $(a_n)$ is stationary and **exponentially mixing** under $\mu$ — this is classical: the Gauss map is a Gibbs–Markov map with exponential decay of correlations.

## Key observation

The digit $1$ occurs with positive probability:
$$p_1 \;=\; \mu(a_1 = 1) \;=\; \log_2\!\Big(1+\tfrac{1}{1\cdot 3}\Big) \;=\; \log_2\!\tfrac{4}{3} \;>\; 0.$$

## Infinitely many $1$'s almost surely

By stationarity, $P(a_n=1)=p_1>0$ for every $n$, so
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(a_n=1) = \infty.$$

By exponential mixing, there exist $C>0$ and $\theta\in(0,1)$ such that for all $m\neq n$:
$$\bigl|P(a_m=1,\; a_n=1) - P(a_m=1)\,P(a_n=1)\bigr| \;\le\; C\,\theta^{|m-n|}.$$

Hence
$$\sum_{m\neq n}\bigl|P(a_m=1,\,a_n=1)-P(a_m=1)P(a_n=1)\bigr| \;<\;\infty.$$

By the **generalized second Borel–Cantelli lemma** (valid for mixing sequences), 
$$P\bigl(a_n=1 \text{ for infinitely many } n\bigr)=1 \quad\text{under }\mu.$$

Since $\mu\equiv\lambda$ (equivalent measures), the same holds under Lebesgue measure:
$$\lambda\bigl(a_n=1 \text{ i.o.}\bigr)=1.$$

## The $1$'s form a divisibility chain

For any $x$ with $a_n(x)=1$ for infinitely many $n$, let $n_1<n_2<n_3<\cdots$ be the positions where $a_{n_k}(x)=1$. Then for every $k$:
$$a_{n_k}=1 \;\mid\; a_{n_{k+1}}=1,$$
since $1\mid 1$. This is an infinite subsequence of the continued fraction digits in which each integer is divisible by the previous one.

Therefore
$$\bigl\{x\in[0,1] : a_n(x)=1 \text{ i.o.}\bigr\} \;\subseteq\; A.$$

Since the set on the left has full Lebesgue measure, we conclude
$$\lambda(A) = 1.$$

## Conclusion

The Lebesgue measure of the Luzin set $A$ is $\boxed{1}$.

### PROOF COMPLETE

## Setup

Every irrational $x\in[0,1]$ has a unique infinite continued fraction expansion $x=[0;\,a_1,a_2,a_3,\dots]$ with $a_i\in\mathbb{N}^+$. Since the rationals have Lebesgue measure $0$, it suffices to work with irrationals.

The **Gauss map** $T(x)=\{1/x\}$ on $(0,1]$ preserves the Gauss measure $\mu$ with density $\frac{1}{\ln 2}\cdot\frac{1}{1+x}$, which is mutually absolutely continuous with Lebesgue measure (with bounded Radon–Nikodym derivative). The continued fraction digits are $a_n = a_1\circ T^{n-1}$, and the sequence $(a_n)$ is stationary and **exponentially mixing** under $\mu$ — this is classical: the Gauss map is a Gibbs–Markov map with exponential decay of correlations.

## Key observation

The digit $1$ occurs with positive probability:
$$p_1 \;=\; \mu(a_1 = 1) \;=\; \log_2\!\Big(1+\tfrac{1}{1\cdot 3}\Big) \;=\; \log_2\!\tfrac{4}{3} \;>\; 0.$$

## Infinitely many $1$'s almost surely

By stationarity, $P(a_n=1)=p_1>0$ for every $n$, so
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} P(a_n=1) = \infty.$$

By exponential mixing, there exist $C>0$ and $\theta\in(0,1)$ such that for all $m\neq n$:
$$\bigl|P(a_m=1,\; a_n=1) - P(a_m=1)\,P(a_n=1)\bigr| \;\le\; C\,\theta^{|m-n|}.$$

Hence
$$\sum_{m\neq n}\bigl|P(a_m=1,\,a_n=1)-P(a_m=1)P(a_n=1)\bigr| \;<\;\infty.$$

By the **generalized second Borel–Cantelli lemma** (valid for mixing sequences), 
$$P\bigl(a_n=1 \text{ for infinitely many } n\bigr)=1 \quad\text{under }\mu.$$

Since $\mu\equiv\lambda$ (equivalent measures), the same holds under Lebesgue measure:
$$\lambda\bigl(a_n=1 \text{ i.o.}\bigr)=1.$$

## The $1$'s form a divisibility chain

For any $x$ with $a_n(x)=1$ for infinitely many $n$, let $n_1<n_2<n_3<\cdots$ be the positions where $a_{n_k}(x)=1$. Then for every $k$:
$$a_{n_k}=1 \;\mid\; a_{n_{k+1}}=1,$$
since $1\mid 1$. This is an infinite subsequence of the continued fraction digits in which each integer is divisible by the previous one.

Therefore
$$\bigl\{x\in[0,1] : a_n(x)=1 \text{ i.o.}\bigr\} \;\subseteq\; A.$$

Since the set on the left has full Lebesgue measure, we conclude
$$\lambda(A) = 1.$$

## Conclusion

The Lebesgue measure of the Luzin set $A$ is $\boxed{1}$.
